10-minute-stress-walk.reason: Strengthen the existing conservative stress-walk protocol with a full-source-reviewed 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and crossover-randomized trials of green exercise. The new evidence supports treating a safe green route as an optional modifier for short-term wellbeing and affect, while preserving the existing boundaries: ten minutes is not an evidence-defined dose, a forest is not required, effects are not guaranteed, and the review does not establish a unique biological mechanism or long-term treatment effect.

lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: When stress is building, consider a short, comfortable walk if walking is safe and practical for you. Treat ten minutes as a convenient boundary, not a medically proven dose. If a greener route is just as easy and safe, prefer it as a reasonable experiment rather than making a special trip. Then notice whether you feel any different before returning to the next task.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I take the walk? Was the route ordinary or relatively green? How did my stress or tension feel before and after, and did I return more able to continue the next task?
lifeOsSource.reference: Liu X, Sun Z, Wang X, Dong D, Samsudin SB. Effects of green exercise on mental health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. 2026;17:1802759.

faq.question: Does the walk need to last exactly 10 minutes?
faq.answer: No. Ten minutes is a convenient practical boundary, not a universal therapeutic dose. The 2026 green-exercise review included varied interventions and did not establish an optimal duration. Choose a duration that is realistic and appropriate for you.

faq.question: Is a park or forest necessary?
faq.answer: No. Randomized studies in the 2026 review used different natural or greener settings, and the review does not justify a route hierarchy for an individual. If a safe tree-lined or greener route is equally convenient, it is reasonable to test it. Do not turn a reset walk into a commute to the perfect forest.

faq.question: Will a green walk always reduce stress immediately?
faq.answer: No. Across randomized and crossover-randomized studies, green exercise improved wellbeing and affect on average compared with non-exercise, indoor exercise and built-up outdoor exercise, but results varied across studies and people. Treat the route choice as a low-cost option, not a guaranteed acute treatment.

faq.question: What should I track in Brali?
faq.answer: Keep it simple: whether you walked, roughly how long, whether the route was relatively green, and how your stress or tension felt before and after. Over several tries, compare whether greener routes seem more useful for you. That is a personal signal, not proof that greenery caused the difference.

intro.html: A short walk can be a simple way to step away from a stressful moment and add some physical activity to the day. A 2026 systematic review of randomized and crossover-randomized trials found that exercise in greener settings improved wellbeing and affect on average compared with non-exercise, indoor exercise and exercise in more built-up outdoor settings. That makes a green route a sensible optional modifier when it is already convenient. It does not make trees a treatment, ten minutes a magic dose, or a forest pilgrimage a productivity requirement.

sections.title: 1. Notice a useful trigger
sections.html: Use a concrete signal such as feeling mentally stuck, tense or overloaded as a cue to consider a short break. The goal is not to diagnose stress or measure it perfectly. The cue only needs to be clear enough to help you decide whether changing context for a few minutes would be useful.

sections.title: 2. Choose the easiest safe route
sections.html: Start with safety and friction. Pick a familiar route that is easy to take now. If two routes are similarly safe and convenient, the 2026 randomized-trial meta-analysis gives you a reason to prefer the greener one. It does not give you a reason to add a long detour, search for a forest, chase a vegetation score or ignore weather and accessibility.

sections.title: 3. Know what the green-route evidence actually says
sections.html: The review pooled 51 randomized or crossover-randomized studies involving 3,092 healthy adults. Green exercise produced better average wellbeing and affect than non-exercise, indoor exercise and exercise in built-up outdoor settings. The comparison is useful, but the studies varied in settings, exercise formats and outcomes, and some pooled results had substantial heterogeneity. The review also does not isolate one mechanism: movement, surroundings, attention, expectations and their interaction are not neatly separated. So the practical claim is modest: when a greener route costs you essentially nothing, it is worth trying.

sections.title: 4. Treat ten minutes as a boundary, not a dose
sections.html: If ten minutes fits the moment, use it as a simple timer. If less time is available, take the shorter walk. The green-exercise review did not establish a minimum effective duration or an optimal dose, and WHO guidance emphasizes that all physical activity counts. Ten minutes is interface convenience, not a biological threshold.

sections.title: 5. Keep the walk simple
sections.html: You do not need a pace target, heart-rate zone, prescribed breathing ratio, forced mindfulness routine or phone ritual for this protocol. Those additions may be useful in other contexts, but they are not required by the evidence reviewed here. Walk comfortably, let the context change happen, then return.

sections.title: 6. Check what happened, not what should have happened
sections.html: Record a quick before-and-after impression of stress or tension and whether returning to the next task felt easier. If you naturally use both ordinary and greener routes, compare them over several attempts. This is an N-of-1 observation, not a causal trial, but it is more useful than assuming an average study effect must apply to you.

sections.title: 7. Know where the evidence stops
sections.html: The review mainly informs short-term mental-health and affect outcomes after green exercise. It does not prove that a short green walk treats depression or anxiety, prevents burnout, improves long-term mental health, or works through a specific nervous-system pathway. If stress is persistent, severe, difficult to cope with or significantly affecting your life, use appropriate professional support rather than relying on this protocol alone. Choose physical activity that is suitable for your health and circumstances.
